items.q: Every correct recursion needs which two parts?
options: A base case that stops, and a recursive case that moves toward the base case

explain.right: The base case is where it stops without calling itself; the recursive case does a bit of work and calls itself on a smaller input, approaching the base case.
explain.wrong: Loops/counters, error handling, and compilers are unrelated to the base/recursive-case structure recursion requires.

items.q: What happens if a recursive function never reaches its base case?
options: It runs faster because there's no stopping check
It keeps calling itself, piling up stack frames until the stack overflows and it crashes

explain.right: Each call adds a stack frame; with no base case they accumulate until the call stack is exhausted (a stack overflow / RecursionError).
explain.wrong: There's no default return, no automatic fix, and runaway recursion crashes rather than speeding up.

items.q: What does the call stack have to do with recursion?
options: Each recursive call pushes a frame holding its own variables; frames pop as calls return
Recursion runs entirely on the heap
Nothing — recursion uses no extra memory
The stack stores the final answer only

explain.right: Every call gets its own stack frame (its locals and return point); they stack up on the way down and pop on the way back up.
explain.wrong: Recursion costs O(n) stack frames for depth n; the stack holds each in-progress call, not just the final answer.

items.q: Which task is recursion most naturally suited to?
options: Walking a tree-shaped structure like nested folders or nested JSON
Summing a flat list of a million numbers

explain.right: Recursion fits naturally recursive/tree-shaped data, where each part contains smaller parts of the same shape.
explain.wrong: Flat, linear, or one-off work is usually clearer and safer with a simple loop or statement than with recursion.

items.q: Give one reason you might rewrite a deep recursion as a loop in Python.
rubric: Notes recursion consumes a stack frame per call (O(n) stack space)
Mentions Python's recursion depth limit / risk of stack overflow (RecursionError) on deep inputs
Concludes a loop avoids that by using constant stack space

explain.right: Good answers cite stack-depth limits / overflow risk and the per-call frame cost, so a loop (O(1) stack) is safer for deep inputs.
explain.wrong: A weak answer says 'loops are just better' with no mention of the stack-depth or memory reason.
